channel.title: LC Insight
channel.description: Crypto market news and on-chain analysis.

item.title: Circle and ACI want banks to settle in USDC on rails they already run. First: Colombia
item.description: ACI Worldwide, which built the core of Colombia's Bre-B instant payment system, will plug Circle's USDC into its payments platform for a Colombian pilot. The two companies gave no volumes, no bank names and no launch date.

item.title: BNB just burned $1.2 billion of itself. Why is 100 million still years away?
item.description: The 37th quarterly auto-burn destroyed 1,646,196 BNB on October 19, the most coins of any burn this year. Supply is now 131.5 million BNB, still 31.5 million above the long-term target.

item.title: bStocks, a Binance affiliate's stock tokens, jumps 53% to $1.31 billion and No. 1
item.description: bStocks, issued on BNB Chain by a Binance group affiliate, is now the largest tokenized stock platform. By our math it added more value in 30 days than the whole $3.58 billion market did, because the rest of the market shrank.

item.title: Zcash NU7 makes blocks 3x faster around November 5. Old nodes will split off
item.description: Zcash's NU7 hard fork activates at block 3,543,405, expected around November 5, 2026. It cuts block time from 75 to 25 seconds without changing supply, sends 60% of fees to a reserve and invalidates version 4 transactions. Nodes that do not upgrade split off.

item.title: How stolen crypto is traced and frozen, and why thieves dump stablecoins fast
item.description: Every blockchain transfer is public, so investigators can follow stolen funds hop by hop. Money can be stopped in two places: stablecoin issuers like Tether and Circle can freeze tokens on-chain, and exchanges can lock accounts when stolen funds arrive.

item.title: Crypto travel rule explained: what exchanges must send with your transfer
item.description: The travel rule requires crypto exchanges and other providers to send the sender's and recipient's details along with a transfer, as banks do with wires. In the EU it applies to every crypto transfer regardless of amount, and 83% of jurisdictions surveyed by the FATF have passed travel rule laws.

item.title: Dubai VARA crypto rules explained: who needs a license and what it covers
item.description: In Dubai, crypto businesses need a license from the Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), which covers the emirate's mainland and free zones except the DIFC. VARA licenses seven activities, from exchanges to custody, and regulates token issuance and crypto marketing.

item.title: Kalshi prices a Democratic sweep at a record 70%. Did a fake pollster move the odds?
item.description: Two days before the November 3 vote, Kalshi's market priced Democrats winning both chambers at 70%, up more than 9 points in a month. Ten days earlier, Kalshi had to explain why a fabricated pollster barely moved its election markets.

item.title: Stablecoins explained: USDT vs. USDC, the two coins that hold 87% of the market
item.description: Stablecoins are tokens built to stay worth $1, backed by reserves such as cash and short-term US government debt. As of November 2, 2026, Tether's USDT ($178.48 billion) and Circle's USDC ($70.68 billion) made up about 87% of a $285.89 billion market, per rwa.xyz.

item.title: What is Sui? The object-based blockchain that says it settles in 390 ms
item.description: Sui is a layer-1 blockchain from Mysten Labs, founded by former Meta engineers, that launched in May 2023. It stores everything as objects with clear owners, runs smart contracts in Move and, by Sui's own figure, settles transactions in roughly 390 milliseconds. SUI has a 10 billion total supply.

item.title: Copy trading explained: how it works, what lead traders take and why results differ
item.description: Copy trading lets you automatically mirror another trader's positions on an exchange, in return for a share of any profit. Your results can differ from theirs because of order size, slippage and timing, and regulators warn it can encourage herd behavior and frequent trading.

item.title: Seed phrase and hardware wallet safety: the words that guard your crypto
item.description: Your seed phrase is the master key to your wallet: anyone who sees it can take everything, and if you lose it, nobody can restore it. A hardware wallet keeps keys offline, but only if the phrase stays offline too and the device is genuine.

item.title: What is DeepSea (desea.io)? The onchain app that labels wallets and tracks flows
item.description: DeepSea (desea.io) is a web app that labels crypto wallets and tracks what smart money, influencers, whales, exchanges and hackers do onchain. It is run by DeepTek Ltd, and its own terms say the data is information only, not financial advice.

item.title: Japan crypto rules explained: FSA registration, 95% cold storage and 2x leverage
item.description: Crypto exchanges in Japan must register with the Financial Services Agency under the Payment Services Act, keep at least 95% of customer coins offline, and cap retail leverage at 2x. A 2026 government bill would revise the rules again, borrowing from securities law.

item.title: Bored Apes are down 96% from their record. Which NFT blue chip fell least?
item.description: Most of the famous NFT collections now sit about 90% to 99% below their peak floor prices in ETH, and the marketplaces are closing. CryptoPunks are the exception, at about 76% down.

item.title: Stellar votes on Bell November 3: wallets must learn a new "W" address
item.description: Stellar's Protocol 30 upgrade, Bell, faces a testnet validator vote on November 3 and a mainnet vote on November 23, 2026. It adds a new "W" address, post-quantum signature checks for smart contracts and millisecond ledger timing, and Stellar says apps must update their SDKs.

item.title: Bitcoin mining and hashrate explained: difficulty, hashprice and data sources
item.description: Bitcoin miners race to find a block hash below a target, and every 2,016 blocks (about two weeks) the network resets the difficulty so blocks keep coming about every 10 minutes. Hashrate, the total guessing power, cannot be measured directly; it is estimated from difficulty and block times.

item.title: What are exchange tokens? BNB keeps burning, OKB froze its supply at 21M
item.description: Exchange tokens are coins tied to a crypto exchange that give holders perks on the platform and pay gas on the exchange's own blockchain. BNB shrinks through quarterly burns toward 100 million; OKB's supply was fixed at 21 million in 2025. Both stay tied to one company.

item.title: What is address poisoning? The copy-paste scam hiding in your wallet history
item.description: Address poisoning is a scam where an attacker plants a lookalike address in your transaction history and waits for you to copy it. No hacking is needed, only a tiny or fake transfer and a hurried user, and the payment cannot be reversed.

item.title: Crypto taxes in the US: Form 1099-DA explained, from proceeds to cost basis
item.description: Form 1099-DA is the IRS form US crypto brokers use to report your sales. It shows gross proceeds for sales from 2025 and adds cost basis for certain sales from 2026, but you must report all crypto gains and income whether or not you get one.

item.title: South Korea crypto rules explained: cold wallets, bank-held cash and jail terms
item.description: Crypto exchanges in South Korea must register with the Financial Intelligence Unit and, since July 19, 2024, follow the Virtual Asset User Protection Act: customer cash held at banks, most coins in cold wallets, and prison terms for market manipulation.

item.title: FDV vs market cap: how to read a token's supply, with HYPE's 4x gap as a guide
item.description: Market cap is price times the tokens circulating today. Fully diluted valuation (FDV) is price times the whole supply, including locked tokens. The gap between them shows how much supply is still to come.

item.title: How to check and revoke token approvals before an old one drains your wallet
item.description: Look up your wallet address in an approval checker such as Etherscan's Token Approvals page or Revoke.cash, find spenders you no longer use or do not recognize, and revoke them. Each revoke is an on-chain transaction, so it costs a small network fee.

item.title: CEX vs DEX explained: who holds your crypto, and what can go wrong
item.description: A centralized exchange (CEX) is a company that holds your coins and matches orders in an order book; a decentralized exchange (DEX) is blockchain software that lets you swap from your own wallet against a pool of tokens. The real trade-off is custody: convenience and support on one side, control and responsibility on the other.

item.title: What is a layer 2? Rollups, proofs and why no big L2 is Stage 2 yet
item.description: A layer 2 is a separate blockchain that runs transactions cheaply and settles them on Ethereum, using fraud proofs or validity proofs to show its state is correct. L2BEAT tracks about $30 billion in L2s, and its Stages show how much control each team still holds.

item.title: One address, two exchange hacks: DeepSea traces where this fall's stolen crypto went
item.description: DeepSea says funds from the Bitget and Binance thefts landed at the same address. Its tracker also shows how little of the loot has reached exchanges, and how much is simply sitting still.

item.title: Prediction markets explained: how Kalshi and Polymarket work, and the real risks
item.description: A prediction market lets people trade contracts that pay $1 if an event happens and $0 if it does not, so prices read like odds. Kalshi is a CFTC-regulated US exchange; most Polymarket markets settle on chain through the UMA oracle.

item.title: Singapore crypto rules explained: who needs a MAS license, and who won't get one
item.description: Crypto firms serving customers in Singapore need a license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, mainly under the Payment Services Act 2019. Since June 30, 2025, Singapore firms that serve only overseas customers also need a license, and MAS says it will generally not grant one.

item.title: Crypto options expiry and max pain explained: what happens at 3 a.m. ET
item.description: Crypto options on Deribit, a major options exchange, expire at 3 a.m. ET (4 a.m. ET during daylight saving time) and settle in cash against a 30-minute average of an index price. Max pain is the strike price at which the most option value would expire worthless, a number traders watch but one that does not control the price.

item.title: Token unlocks explained: cliffs, vesting and why unlocked does not mean sold
item.description: A token unlock is when tokens locked at launch, usually for the team, investors or a treasury, become free to move. Unlocks add to circulating supply and dilute holders, but an unlocked token is not a sold one: Hyperliquid insiders claimed far less HYPE than they could.

item.title: What is a wallet drainer? How one signature can empty your crypto wallet
item.description: A wallet drainer is a scam kit that tricks you into signing an approval or permit that lets the attacker move your tokens. Your seed phrase never leaves your hands: your own signature does the damage, sometimes days later.

item.title: Bitcoin dominance and crypto market cap explained: why sites say 58% or 60%
item.description: Total crypto market cap adds up the market value of every tracked coin, and bitcoin dominance is bitcoin's share of it. As of November 2, 2026, the total was about $2.6 trillion to $2.7 trillion and bitcoin's share about 58% to 60%, depending on the data site.

item.title: Hong Kong crypto licensing explained: SFC exchange rules, 2 of 36 stablecoin bids
item.description: In Hong Kong, crypto exchanges need a license from the Securities and Futures Commission, and anyone issuing a fiat-backed stablecoin needs one from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. Only two stablecoin issuers had been licensed as of April 2026: HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial.

item.title: SEC vs. CFTC: who regulates crypto in the US, and where the line now falls
item.description: The SEC oversees crypto that counts as a security, and the CFTC oversees commodities like bitcoin and ether plus derivatives on them. Since March 2026, the two agencies share an interpretation that says most crypto assets are not securities.

item.title: Binance Launchpool and HODLer Airdrops explained: how BNB holders earn new tokens
item.description: Launchpool pays a new token hour by hour to people who lock BNB or stablecoins; HODLer Airdrops pay one after the fact to people who held BNB in Simple Earn during a past window. Both depend on your share of a pool, and both carry price risk.

item.title: Ethereum roadmap explained: Pectra, Fusaka and why Glamsterdam has no date
item.description: Ethereum upgrades through named hard forks. Pectra went live on May 7, 2025, and Fusaka on December 3, 2025. Glamsterdam, the next one, is live on the Sepolia testnet but was pulled from Hoodi in October 2026, and as of November 2, 2026, it has no mainnet date.

item.title: Tokenized Treasuries explained: BUIDL, USDY and the $14.2B T-bill market
item.description: Tokenized Treasuries are blockchain tokens that stand for shares in funds holding US government debt, and unlike most stablecoins they pay interest. As of November 2, 2026, rwa.xyz counted $14.21 billion across 119 products, led by Ondo's USDY, Circle's USYC and BlackRock's BUIDL.

item.title: What is a TGE? Token launch day explained, and why most supply stays locked
item.description: A TGE, or token generation event, is the moment a crypto project creates its token and the first slice starts to circulate. Airdrop claims and trading usually begin then, while team and investor tokens stay locked for months or years.

item.title: Bitcoin halving explained: what it is, when the next one is and why it matters
item.description: The bitcoin halving is a rule in bitcoin's code that cuts the reward for mining a new block in half every 210,000 blocks, about every four years. The last one happened on April 20, 2024, at block 840,000. The next is due at block 1,050,000, expected around spring 2028.

item.title: How crypto exchange hacks happen: the weak spot is rarely the key itself
item.description: Most exchange hacks start in hot wallets, the online wallets that pay out withdrawals. Attackers rarely break the cryptography. They get into the systems and people that approve transactions, then rush to swap stablecoins before issuers can freeze them.

item.title: Binance took in 18,435 BTC in two weeks while $6.81 billion in stablecoins walked out
item.description: DeepSea's data shows about $1.5 billion in bitcoin flowing into Binance in early October, just as billions in USDT left. Kraken saw the opposite, and the price fell anyway.

item.title: Doppler's XDP is trending again, with daily volume 95% below launch week. What is it?
item.description: Doppler Finance's XDP token sat fourth on DeepSea's 24-hour trending list late on November 1 (ET), a month after launch. CoinGecko shows it hit a record low on October 30, and DeepSea finds the top 10 wallets hold 95% of supply.

item.title: Vietnam crypto law explained: 5 licenses, VND 200M fines and a 6-month clock
item.description: Crypto is legally defined in Vietnam, and a five-year pilot lets up to five licensed local firms run crypto markets. As of the latest official update on October 6, 2026, no provider had been licensed, so the six-month countdown for investors using unlicensed platforms has not started.

item.title: What is restaking? EigenLayer explained, from extra rewards to slashing risk
item.description: Restaking lets stakers put the same stake to work securing extra services for extra rewards. EigenLayer is the main protocol for it: stakers deposit assets, operators run the services, and those services can slash stake when rules are broken.

item.title: How crypto liquidations work: why a 10% move can wipe out a 10x trade
item.description: A liquidation is when an exchange force-closes a leveraged trade because losses have eaten through the trader's collateral. It protects the exchange and other traders from debts the trader cannot pay.

item.title: AI agents in crypto explained: how bots get wallets and pay, and what can go wrong
item.description: An AI agent is software that takes actions on its own, not just answers questions. In crypto, agents hold wallets and pay for things in stablecoins, often through the x402 protocol, with spending limits their owners may or may not switch on.

item.title: What are points programs in crypto? How they work and why points are not tokens
item.description: A points program scores what users do on a crypto product, such as deposits, trades or referrals, and usually hints that points will later become tokens. Points are not tokens: the project decides if, when and how they convert.

item.title: What is Solana? Alpenglow explained, from 12.8-second finality to a 150 ms goal
item.description: Alpenglow is Solana's new consensus protocol. Its first part, Votor, went live on mainnet on October 21, 2026, replacing TowerBFT and cutting the time for a transaction to become final from about 12.8 seconds to a target of about 150 milliseconds.

item.title: CLARITY Act explained: what the crypto market bill would do and why it stalled
item.description: The CLARITY Act, H.R. 3633, would write into law which crypto assets and platforms the SEC oversees and which fall to the CFTC. As of November 2, 2026, it is stuck in the Senate after a 49 to 50 vote to start debate failed on September 15.

item.title: Perpetual futures funding rates explained: how 0.05% can cost 55% a year
item.description: A funding rate is a small payment that traders of perpetual futures make to each other to keep the contract's price close to the real market price. When it is positive, longs pay shorts. When it is negative, shorts pay longs.
